versions.title: The breath-hold challenge
versions.blurb: A dangerous "challenge" is spreading fast on a Friday evening. Contain it without wrecking your weekend team or silencing the people warning against it.

steps.s: On-call reviewers have seen 40 videos in two hours showing teens holding their breath until they nearly pass out. The hashtag is growing about 300% an hour. A news site abroad has reported a hospitalization linked to it. Your dangerous-acts policy covers this, but nobody has formally classified the trend.

o.l: Restrict the hashtag and related searches now, add a safety interstitial, and start a targeted content sweep.
o.r: Distribution drops within the hour. A few creators complain that their search results changed.

o.l: Log it for Monday's policy review. The policy question should be settled before you act.
o.r: The hashtag triples over the weekend. By Monday it is trending in three countries.

o.l: Remove every video using the hashtag, including news reports and parents' warnings.
o.r: Reach falls, but journalists and parent groups say they were silenced. Appeals start piling up.

steps.lesson: Contain distribution first (search, hashtags, recommendations), then refine enforcement. Protect counter-speech and news coverage. Over-removal creates a second incident.
steps.law: The UK Online Safety Act lists content encouraging dangerous stunts and challenges as “priority content” harmful to children. Services likely to be accessed by children must protect them from it.

steps.s: About 12,000 related uploads are waiting. Your overnight shift can handle about 2,000. A near-duplicate matcher could be ready in 45 minutes. The graphic-violence and child-safety queues are also staffed tonight.

o.l: Deploy near-duplicate matching to auto-action clear copies. Prioritize everything else for human review by reach.
o.r: The highest-reach videos are reviewed first. QA later finds about 3% false positives, which are restored on appeal.

o.l: Move reviewers off the other queues, including child safety, so every video gets a human look.
o.r: The trend queue clears, but child-safety SLAs are missed overnight. That will come up in your next audit.

o.l: Remove the videos from recommendations and wait until Monday to review them.
o.r: Discovery slows, but the videos still spread through shares and direct links.

steps.lesson: Prioritize by potential reach, not by arrival order. Never pull staff from your highest-severity queues to cover a louder incident.

steps.h: Press and parents are asking questions
steps.s: A national reporter wants comment by 15:00. A large parents' group has tagged your company in a thread that is going viral. Your Comms lead is on a flight.

o.l: With Legal and a Comms backup, send a short factual statement: what you're seeing, what you've done, and resources for parents.
o.r: The story quotes your statement and links to your parent resources. The thread calms down.

o.l: Say "no comment" until the investigation is finished.
o.r: The headline reads "Platform silent as dangerous trend spreads".

o.l: Publish detailed removal numbers and explain exactly how your detection works.
o.r: People like the transparency. By Sunday, uploaders are altering their videos to evade the matcher.

steps.lesson: Say quickly what you know and what you're doing. Share outcomes, not detection methods, while the trend is still active.

steps.s: Uploads have dropped 85% from their peak. Your team is exhausted. Executives want to know whether this will happen again.

o.l: Hold a blameless post-incident review covering detection time, gaps and false positives. Add the trend to monitoring and brief executives with numbers.
o.r: You leave with three concrete fixes, including a trend watchlist, and a team that feels heard.

o.l: Lift the restrictions and return to normal work.
o.r: Two weeks later a variant appears under a new hashtag, and you start from scratch.

o.l: Leave every emergency measure in place permanently to be safe.
o.r: Unrelated breath-work and freediving creators keep getting suppressed. Complaints continue.

steps.lesson: Emergency measures need an end date and a review. The post-incident review is what makes the next incident smaller.
steps.law: For very large platforms, the EU Digital Services Act (Articles 34 and 35) requires yearly systemic-risk assessments covering harm to minors. Post-incident reviews feed directly into them.

versions.title: The regulator's request
versions.blurb: An EU regulator asks how your recommender exposes minors to eating-disorder content. You have ten working days, and your data has gaps.

steps.h: A formal request for information arrives
steps.s: The regulator is asking how your recommendation systems affect teen users' exposure to eating-disorder content, what risk assessment you did, and which mitigations are in place. The deadline is ten working days. Legal forwarded it to you with the note "thoughts?"

o.l: Set up a cross-functional response team (Legal, Policy, Data Science, Product) with one owner, and map every question to a data source.
o.r: By day 1 you know which questions you can answer and which ones you can't.

o.l: Leave it to Legal and offer to help if they ask.
o.r: On day 7 Legal asks for "all the data" and the scramble begins.

o.l: Request an extension right away, before scoping the work.
o.r: The regulator asks why you need one. You can't say yet.

steps.lesson: A regulator's request is a T&S data problem that Legal packages. Assign one owner and map every question to a source on day 0.
steps.law: Under the EU Digital Services Act (Article 67), the European Commission can send formal requests for information to very large platforms. Supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information can be fined up to 1% of annual worldwide turnover.

steps.s: Data Science reports that your last prevalence measurement for eating-disorder content is 14 months old. Your teen-age signals are also known to miss a large share of under-18 users.

o.l: Disclose the limitations, provide the best available data with its methodology, and commit to a dated plan to fix it.
o.r: Regulators ask follow-up questions, but they treat you as a credible partner.

o.l: Report only the metrics that look good and leave the gaps out.
o.r: A later audit finds the gap. Your credibility is gone, and your fine exposure rises sharply.

o.l: Rush a new prevalence study using a small sample in four days.
o.r: You get numbers, but the confidence intervals are wide and the team works through the weekend.

steps.lesson: Regulators forgive known gaps with a remediation plan far more readily than figures that later turn out to be misleading.
steps.law: Supplying misleading information to a DSA request is itself a finable breach, separate from any underlying risk.

steps.h: Product pushes back on the fix
steps.s: Your proposed fix is to stop recommending weight-loss content to teen accounts by default. The Product lead objects because modeling shows a 2% drop in teen session time.

o.l: Escalate with a risk case: estimated harm, regulatory exposure and fine ceiling. Propose a staged rollout with a guardrail metric.
o.r: Your VP backs a staged launch. The mitigation goes in the submission as live.

o.l: Drop the fix to keep the peace.
o.r: Your submission has no mitigations, which is exactly what the regulator was checking for.

o.l: Ship it yourself using T&S ranking controls, without Product sign-off.
o.r: It works, but Product rolls it back in an unrelated release and trust between the teams collapses.

steps.lesson: Directors win these arguments by making risk as concrete as the engagement cost, and by offering a staged path rather than an all-or-nothing choice.
steps.law: DSA Article 28 requires platforms accessible to minors to ensure a high level of privacy, safety and security; Article 35 requires very large platforms to mitigate systemic risks.

steps.s: The response is drafted. Leadership wants to know what happens next.

o.l: Submit an honest risk assessment and a dated mitigation roadmap, and track the commitments internally like an OKR.
o.r: Six months later the follow-up request is short, because you hit your dates.

o.l: Submit and consider the matter closed.
o.r: The follow-up asks about commitments nobody tracked.

o.l: Publish a blog post announcing the new teen protections before you submit.
o.r: The press coverage is good. The regulator reads it as an attempt to get ahead of the process.

steps.lesson: Treat commitments to regulators as roadmap items with owners and dates. The follow-up request will test them.

versions.title: The special-treatment leak
versions.blurb: A journalist has screenshots suggesting high-profile accounts get slower, softer enforcement. They want comment within 24 hours.

steps.h: A journalist has your internal screenshots
steps.s: The screenshots show violations by a celebrity account sent to a "sensitive accounts" queue and left up for weeks, while ordinary users were removed within hours for similar posts. The deadline is 24 hours.

o.l: Verify the facts first: pull the case histories and queue data, and bring in Comms and Legal.
o.r: Within six hours you know exactly what happened and how bad it is.

o.l: Tell Comms the program doesn't exist.
o.r: It does exist. The follow-up story is about the denial.

o.l: Remove the celebrity's posts immediately to get ahead of the story.
o.r: The journalist now reports that you enforce reactively when caught.

steps.lesson: In the first hours, the only job is establishing the facts. Anything you say before you know them becomes the next story.

steps.s: Three of the five posts did violate policy. The sensitive-accounts queue has a median time to action of 19 days, compared with 9 hours for the standard queue. It has no owner and no SLA.

o.l: Act on the three violations under standard policy now, and acknowledge the SLA gap internally.
o.r: The account gets the same strike anyone else would. Your team sees the rules applied evenly.

o.l: Leave it. High-profile accounts need extra care.
o.r: The published story shows the posts are still up.

o.l: Ban the account permanently to show you are serious.
o.r: Your penalty rules called for a strike. You are now accused of overcorrecting.

steps.lesson: Consistency means the same penalty rules for everyone, not the harshest action for whoever is in the news.
steps.law: The EU Digital Services Act (Article 14) requires platforms to apply their terms diligently, objectively and proportionately. Slower, softer enforcement for high-profile accounts can breach this.

steps.s: Comms needs your input on the statement.

o.l: Acknowledge the gap. Explain why extra review exists (to prevent errors on high-reach accounts) and commit to matching SLAs and outside oversight.
o.r: The story runs with your commitment in the third paragraph, and the reaction is mixed but manageable.

o.l: Say a single moderator made a mistake.
o.r: Screenshots show it was systemic. Your moderators see you blame one of them.

o.l: Decline to comment.
o.r: The piece runs unchallenged.

steps.lesson: Explain why the process exists, own where it failed, and never make a front-line employee the explanation for a systemic gap.

steps.s: Leadership asks you for a permanent fix.

o.l: Keep the extra review but within the standard SLA, log every override, and report the volumes in your transparency report.
o.r: The process now protects against errors without being a way around the rules.

o.l: Remove all special handling for high-profile accounts.
o.r: A month later, a wrong takedown on a head of state's account becomes its own incident.

o.l: Rename the queue and tighten access.
o.r: The next leak includes the rename.

steps.lesson: Extra review for high-reach accounts is defensible. An exemption from the rules is not. The difference is SLAs, logging and transparency.
steps.law: DSA transparency reports (Articles 15 and 24) must describe how moderation works. Disclosing special review programs protects you when they come to light.

versions.title: The counterfeit flood
versions.blurb: A luxury brand's lawyers demand that 1,400 listings come down in 48 hours, days before your biggest sales event.

steps.h: A brand's legal team sends a demand
steps.s: A luxury brand has listed 1,400 listings it says are counterfeit and threatens to sue if they aren't removed in 48 hours. Your Black Friday sale starts Thursday. Spot checks suggest about 70% are clear fakes; the rest are genuine resale or unclear.

o.l: Remove all 1,400 immediately to make the problem go away.
o.r: The brand is satisfied, but hundreds of legitimate resellers lose sales, flood support and post about it.

o.l: Remove clear fakes now, hold unclear listings for joint review with the brand, and tell sellers why.
o.r: Most fakes are down within a day. The brand's counsel accepts the plan and genuine resellers keep selling.

o.l: Ask the brand to file individual notices through your standard IP form.
o.r: It's defensible, but the brand goes public and the fakes stay up through the sale.

steps.lesson: Pressure from a rights holder doesn't remove the need for accuracy. Act fast on clear cases, review the unclear ones, and explain decisions to sellers.
steps.law: Notice-and-action rules (EU DSA Article 16) require timely, diligent and objective decisions on notices, not blanket removal. In the US, trademark takedowns aren't covered by the DMCA's safe harbor, so an accurate, documented process matters.

steps.h: The same sellers keep coming back
steps.s: Removed sellers are relisting within hours under new accounts, with the same photos and shipping addresses. Your seller checks only verify an email address.

o.l: Ban each new account as reports come in.
o.r: Reviewers spend the day chasing relists while new ones appear.

o.l: Pause all new listings in the affected categories for the week.
o.r: The fakes stop, and so do legitimate new sellers in the biggest sales week of the year.

o.l: Link accounts by photo hashes, shipping addresses and payout details, and remove the whole network.
o.r: One sweep removes 60 linked accounts, and relisting slows sharply.

steps.lesson: Counterfeiters operate as networks. Remove the network using shared signals instead of chasing single listings.

steps.s: About 900 buyers have already received fakes. Some want refunds, and a consumer group says you're profiting from counterfeits.

o.l: Refund affected buyers proactively and recover the money from held seller payouts.
o.r: Held payouts cover most refunds, and the consumer group acknowledges the response.

o.l: Tell buyers to take it up with the sellers directly.
o.r: The sellers have vanished. Buyers go to their banks and chargebacks pile up.

o.l: Refund only buyers who complain publicly.
o.r: It quiets the loudest voices, until a screenshot of the policy leaks.

steps.lesson: Buyer protection is part of your promise. Holding payouts for new sellers is what makes it affordable to make buyers whole.

steps.s: The sale is over. The brand wants a standing agreement, and your CEO wants to know why this happened.

o.l: Give the brand direct takedown access to your listings.
o.r: Takedowns are fast, but the brand starts removing legitimate resale and you face complaints and legal risk.

o.l: Launch a brand protection program: a verified rights-holder portal, a repeat-infringer policy and stronger checks in high-risk categories.
o.r: Takedowns get faster and more accurate, and fakes drop before the holidays.

o.l: Treat it as a one-off and move on.
o.r: The same networks return for the next sale.

steps.lesson: Rights holders are partners, not moderators. A structured program with accuracy checks protects both brands and legitimate sellers.
steps.law: Under the DSA (Article 22), notices from officially designated trusted flaggers get priority, but the platform still makes the decision.

versions.title: The too-good-to-be-true listings
versions.blurb: Scammers post cheap consoles and phones, then move buyers off the platform to pay by bank transfer.

steps.s: Support has 200 reports this week: buyers paid by bank transfer for consoles that never arrived. The listings are new, priced 40% below market, and the seller's first message asks buyers to “pay outside the app to avoid fees”.

o.l: Warn buyers when a message mentions bank transfers or other apps, and hold new sellers' high-value listings for review.
o.r: Reports fall by half within two days.

o.l: Publish a blog post about staying safe from scams.
o.r: A few people read it. The scams continue.

o.l: Block every mention of payment methods in messages.
o.r: Scammers switch to code words within hours, and legitimate users are confused by blocked messages.

steps.lesson: Intervene in the conversation, at the moment of risk, and add friction where the pattern concentrates: new sellers with cheap high-value items.
steps.law: Fraud is a priority illegal harm under the UK Online Safety Act, so platforms must assess and reduce scam risk proactively, not only respond to reports.

steps.s: Victims paid outside your checkout, so buyer protection doesn't technically apply. Several are older users who lost more than $1,000.

o.l: Refuse: they paid off-platform, against your terms.
o.r: Victims share their stories, and the headline is about your refusal.

o.l: Refund everyone who claims to be a victim.
o.r: It's costly, and fraudsters start filing fake victim claims.

o.l: Make one-time goodwill payments to clearly deceived victims, help them report to their bank and police, and share evidence with law enforcement.
o.r: Victims feel supported, and police link dozens of cases.

steps.lesson: “They broke our terms” is rarely a good public answer. Targeted goodwill plus help recovering funds builds trust without inviting fraud.

steps.s: The same group now uses established accounts with good reviews, hijacked and bought on a forum.

o.l: Require ID verification for every seller, starting today.
o.r: Fraud drops, but thousands of legitimate sellers abandon verification.

o.l: Detect sudden changes on established accounts: new devices, new payout details, a burst of cheap high-value listings.
o.r: You catch 30 hijacked accounts in a day and return many to their real owners.

o.l: Keep reviewing reports manually.
o.r: The queue grows and scams keep landing.

steps.lesson: Account takeover turns your trust signals against you. Watch for behavior changes on trusted accounts, not only on new ones.

steps.s: Leadership asks what should change for good.

o.l: Remove messaging between buyers and sellers.
o.r: Scams drop, and so do sales. Product reverses it within a month.

o.l: Add a line to the terms of service.
o.r: Nothing changes.

o.l: Make protected in-app checkout the default for high-value items, with a clear warning on anything off-platform.
o.r: Most high-value sales move into protected checkout, and scam losses fall sharply.

steps.lesson: Safe defaults built into the transaction beat warnings and terms. Make the protected path the easy one.

versions.title: The money mule network
versions.blurb: Young customers are receiving and instantly forwarding stolen money. Many were recruited on social media.

steps.s: 180 accounts opened last month share a pattern: many incoming payments from strangers, forwarded within minutes to a few crypto exchanges. Most holders are 18 to 21. Two banks have flagged payments to these accounts as fraud.

o.l: Watch for another week to gather more evidence.
o.r: Another $600,000 of victims' money moves through before you act.

o.l: Freeze all 180 accounts and file suspicious activity reports.
o.r: The flow of stolen money stops. Some innocent customers are caught up and need a fast review path.

o.l: Close the accounts quietly and send the money back to the senders.
o.r: Returning funds without investigation sends some of it straight to the fraudsters' other accounts.

steps.lesson: Stop the flow first, then investigate. Freezing and reporting is both a legal duty and the fastest way to protect victims.
steps.law: In the US, the Bank Secrecy Act generally requires a suspicious activity report within 30 days of detecting suspicious activity. The UK and EU have equivalent reporting duties, and tipping off the subject can be an offence.

steps.s: Interviews show many account holders were promised “easy money” online and didn't know the money was stolen. Parents are calling support.

o.l: Separate recruiters from recruits: offboard the organizers, and give recruits a warning, education and a monitored way back.
o.r: Most recruits cooperate, and a few identify the recruiters.

o.l: Close every account holder's account permanently.
o.r: It's allowed, but students lose access to banking and the press calls it cruel.

o.l: Unfreeze anyone who says they didn't know.
o.r: Recruiters coach their mules to say exactly that.

steps.lesson: Money-mule networks exploit young people. Tell organizers apart from recruits, and pair enforcement with education.

steps.s: The recruitment posts are on a large social platform and a messaging app, using your brand name: “get paid through [your app]”.

o.l: Report the posts with each platform's public report button.
o.r: A few come down after a week. Most stay up.

o.l: Threaten legal action against the platforms.
o.r: Their legal teams respond slowly and nothing changes this month.

o.l: Share indicators with the platforms' trust & safety teams and your banking partners, and warn your customers.
o.r: The platforms remove hundreds of posts, and banks block linked accounts.

steps.lesson: Fraud crosses platforms. Relationships for sharing intelligence, built before a crisis, are what make cross-platform takedowns fast.

steps.s: Your regulator asks how you'll stop this happening again.

o.l: Add velocity rules for new accounts that receive from many senders and forward money quickly, with extra checks when they trigger.
o.r: New mule accounts are caught within days instead of weeks.

o.l: Stop letting under-21s open accounts.
o.r: Fraud drops a little. Young customers go elsewhere, and you face age-discrimination questions.

o.l: Rely on your bank partners to catch it.
o.r: The regulator is unimpressed: mule monitoring is your job.

steps.lesson: Mule detection is behavioral: money in from many people, money out fast. Build it into monitoring rather than targeting demographics.
steps.law: Regulators expect transaction monitoring proportionate to your risk, for example under FinCEN rules in the US and the UK Money Laundering Regulations 2017.

versions.title: The fake fraud team
versions.blurb: Scammers are calling customers pretending to be your fraud team and persuading them to move savings to a “safe account”.

steps.s: In two days, 60 customers sent their savings to “safe accounts” after calls from people claiming to be your fraud team, using a spoofed version of your phone number. Losses average $8,000.

o.l: Wait until Monday to agree a statement with Comms.
o.r: Another 90 customers lose money over the weekend.

o.l: Block all transfers over $1,000 temporarily.
o.r: Scam losses stop, but thousands of customers can't pay rent or bills.

o.l: Send an urgent in-app alert to every customer: “We will never ask you to move money to a safe account.”
o.r: Calls continue, but many customers hang up. Reported losses drop by two-thirds over the weekend.

steps.lesson: In an active scam wave, speed of warning matters most. Tell customers exactly what you will never ask them to do.

steps.s: A customer is trying to send their entire balance to a new payee, minutes after an incoming call. They insist it's urgent.

o.l: Let it go through: it's the customer's money.
o.r: It's a scam. The customer loses $22,000, and reimbursement rules may make you pay.

o.l: Pause the payment and have a trained agent call back on a verified number, asking questions designed to break the scammer's script.
o.r: The customer realizes it's a scam and thanks you.

o.l: Freeze the whole account.
o.r: The scam is stopped, but so are the customer's real bills, and they're angry.

steps.lesson: Targeted friction at the riskiest moment works best, especially friction that breaks the social-engineering script.

steps.s: 150 victims want reimbursement. Some were careless; others were elderly and fooled by a spoofed number.

o.l: Reimburse using a clear policy based on vulnerability and how convincing the scam was, and recover a share from the receiving banks.
o.r: Most victims are reimbursed quickly, and receiving banks share the cost.

o.l: Refuse all claims because customers authorized the payments.
o.r: In the UK this breaks reimbursement rules; elsewhere it becomes a headline.

o.l: Reimburse everyone in full, no questions asked.
o.r: Victims are grateful. Within a month, fraudsters start staging fake scam claims.

steps.lesson: Reimbursement needs a consistent, documented policy that protects vulnerable customers without rewarding fake claims.
steps.law: Since October 2024, UK payment firms must reimburse most authorised push payment scam victims up to £85,000, splitting the cost 50:50 between sending and receiving firms. There's an exception for gross negligence by the customer.

steps.s: The scammers spoofed your number and used customer details from an old data breach.

o.l: Change your support phone number.
o.r: Scammers spoof the new one within a week.

o.l: Work with phone carriers to block spoofing of your numbers, and show in the app when a call really is from you.
o.r: Impersonation calls drop sharply.

o.l: Tell customers to be more careful in your newsletter.
o.r: Few people read it.

steps.lesson: Impersonation scams need channel fixes: authenticated calls, carrier partnerships and in-app confirmation.
steps.law: Caller authentication programs such as STIR/SHAKEN in the US, and similar schemes elsewhere, help carriers block spoofed calls that impersonate trusted brands.

versions.title: The gifts that weren't gifts
versions.blurb: A parent reports an adult who befriended their 11-year-old in your game with in-game gifts, then moved the chat to another app.

steps.s: A parent emails that an adult player gifted their 11-year-old in-game currency for weeks, then asked them to chat on another app and send photos. They have screenshots. The adult's account is still active.

o.l: Reply that you'll look into it within your standard three-day review time.
o.r: The account keeps messaging children for three more days.

o.l: Escalate now: suspend the account, preserve chats and gift records, and report to NCMEC or the police.
o.r: The account is stopped within the hour, and evidence is preserved for investigators.

o.l: Ban the account and delete its data.
o.r: The account is stopped, but the evidence police need is gone.

steps.lesson: Child-safety reports need their own fast lane. Suspend, preserve evidence and report. Never delete evidence.
steps.law: US law (18 U.S.C. § 2258A) requires reporting apparent child sexual exploitation to NCMEC's CyberTipline. The 2024 REPORT Act added online enticement to the reporting duty and extended evidence preservation to one year.

steps.s: The account's gift history shows currency sent to 40 other child accounts, and it's linked by device to six other adult accounts.

o.l: Ban the linked accounts and close the case.
o.r: The other children who were contacted never get support.

o.l: Wait for other parents to report.
o.r: Few children report. The harm stays hidden.

o.l: Review all 40 conversations and the six linked accounts, and contact the affected families through their parent accounts.
o.r: You find two more children who were asked for images, and their families can act.

steps.lesson: One report is often the tip of a pattern. Follow the network and reach the other children affected.

steps.s: Your data shows adults gifting currency to children they aren't connected to is rare, but strongly linked to confirmed grooming cases.

o.l: Block gifts from adults to children they aren't connected to, and flag attempts for review.
o.r: The lure is closed with little effect on normal play.

o.l: Turn off gifting for everyone.
o.r: The lure is gone, but so is a feature families love, and revenue dips.

o.l: Keep gifting as it is: it's core to the game.
o.r: Two months later, the pattern appears again.

steps.lesson: Remove the specific mechanics predators exploit, targeting risky combinations rather than whole features.

steps.s: Parents are worried, and a news outlet asks whether your game is safe for children.

o.l: Say you have “zero tolerance” and decline to give details.
o.r: The reporter notes you didn't describe any changes.

o.l: Say the incident was isolated and rare.
o.r: Two more parents come forward the next day.

o.l: Launch parental controls (chat off by default for under-13s, gift limits, activity summaries) and explain them clearly.
o.r: Parents adopt the controls, and the coverage mentions them.

steps.lesson: Give parents real controls and honest explanations. Reassurance without action backfires.
steps.law: In 2022 the FTC fined Epic Games $275 million under COPPA, citing voice and text chat switched on by default for children. The UK Age Appropriate Design Code also expects high-privacy defaults for children.

versions.title: The swatting threat
versions.blurb: A popular streamer is hit by a coordinated harassment campaign that escalates to posting their home address.

steps.s: A streamer with 500,000 followers is being flooded with slurs in voice and text chat across dozens of matches. Hundreds of brand-new accounts are involved.

o.l: Limit new accounts from joining the streamer's matches, tighten chat filters in those lobbies, and ban the organizing accounts.
o.r: The flood slows within the hour.

o.l: Tell the streamer to use the block button.
o.r: They can't block hundreds of accounts mid-match. The campaign continues.

o.l: Turn off chat across the whole game for the night.
o.r: The harassment stops, and so does everyone else's game.

steps.lesson: Coordinated harassment needs coordinated defenses: limits on new accounts, targeted filtering and action against organizers.

steps.s: Someone posts the streamer's home address in match chat and on a forum, saying they'll “send a SWAT team”.

o.l: Remove the post and ban the account.
o.r: The post is gone, but police aren't warned.

o.l: Wait until Monday for your legal team.
o.r: A SWAT team arrives at the streamer's home at 3 a.m.

o.l: Remove the content, preserve evidence, warn local police about a possible swatting call, and tell the streamer.
o.r: Police flag the address, and a hoax call later that night is handled calmly.

steps.lesson: Threats to physical safety need a 24/7 emergency path to law enforcement.
steps.law: US law (18 U.S.C. § 2702(b)(8)) lets providers disclose data to law enforcement when they believe in good faith that an emergency involves danger of death or serious injury. Many other countries have similar emergency provisions.

steps.s: The attackers organized in a server on another chat platform and used your game's party system to coordinate.

o.l: Ban only the accounts that sent slurs.
o.r: The organizers regroup under new accounts.

o.l: Share the organizing accounts with the other platform's trust & safety team and ban the linked accounts in your game.
o.r: The other platform removes the server, and the campaign collapses.

o.l: Name the organizers publicly.
o.r: The feud escalates, and the organizers gain followers.

steps.lesson: Harassment is usually organized somewhere else. Cross-platform cooperation and action against organizers break campaigns.

steps.s: Other streamers ask what you'll do to protect them.

o.l: Say harassment comes with being online.
o.r: Creators leave for a competitor.

o.l: Pay creators to keep streaming.
o.r: Some stay, but they're still unprotected.

o.l: Start a creator safety program: priority escalation, lobby protections and private support.
o.r: Creators feel supported, and several who planned to leave stay.

steps.lesson: Highly visible users attract concentrated abuse. A dedicated escalation path costs little and builds a lot of trust.

versions.title: The date that went wrong
versions.blurb: A user reports being sexually assaulted by a match. The accused is still active and has more dates lined up.

steps.s: A user reports that a match sexually assaulted her on a first date last night. She has told the police. The accused's account is active, and he has three dates arranged this week.

o.l: Ask her for proof before you act.
o.r: She stops responding. The accused goes on his dates.

o.l: Warn his upcoming matches that someone has reported him.
o.r: It may breach privacy and defamation law, and the warning leaks.

o.l: Suspend the accused while you investigate, support the reporter with resources, and preserve evidence for police.
o.r: No further dates happen, and police ask for the preserved data.

steps.lesson: For serious offline-harm reports, suspend during the investigation, support the person who reported, and preserve evidence.
steps.law: In the US, law enforcement can ask providers to preserve records for 90 days, renewable (18 U.S.C. § 2703(f)). For serious offline harm, preserve evidence proactively instead of waiting to be asked.

steps.s: The accused says it was consensual and threatens to sue. Police are investigating but won't share details.

o.l: Keep the suspension under your safety policy, which allows action on credible reports without a criminal conviction.
o.r: His lawyer backs off after reading your policy.

o.l: Reinstate him until the police finish.
o.r: He matches with more users, and a second report arrives.

o.l: Delete his account and data immediately.
o.r: The police investigation loses important evidence.

steps.lesson: Your safety standard isn't a criminal court's. A clear policy lets you act on credible risk while preserving evidence.
steps.law: Platforms can enforce their own safety policies without a criminal conviction, as long as the terms are clear and applied consistently.

steps.s: A new account with different photos, but the same phone number and device, starts matching in the same area.

o.l: Require ID checks for everyone in that city.
o.r: He's blocked, but so are many real users, who drop off.

o.l: Ban the new account and link it to the original case.
o.r: You block him again within hours, and the case record stays complete.

o.l: Wait for a new report.
o.r: He goes on a date before anyone reports him.

steps.lesson: Ban evasion is predictable after serious bans. Device, phone and payment signals make repeat offenders catchable.

steps.s: A journalist investigating assaults linked to dating apps asks what you do to prevent them.

o.l: Explain your safety features (photo verification, date check-ins, how reports are handled) and publish safety numbers.
o.r: The article names you as one of the more responsive apps.

o.l: Point them to your community guidelines.
o.r: The story says you “declined to explain”.

o.l: Offer an exclusive on a new feature launch instead.
o.r: The reporter sees it as deflection.

steps.lesson: Offline harm is the defining risk for dating apps. Be ready to explain prevention and response in specifics.

versions.title: The romance scam ring
versions.blurb: An organized ring is running romance and investment scams through your app with AI-generated profiles.

steps.s: Reports of users being pushed into crypto “investments” after weeks of chatting have tripled. Many suspect profiles use flawless AI-generated photos and near-identical opening lines.

o.l: Remove reported profiles one at a time.
o.r: New profiles appear faster than you can remove them.

o.l: Suspend every profile without a verification badge.
o.r: Scams drop, and so do half your real users' matches.

o.l: Cluster the profiles by shared signals (generated-photo traits, scripts, devices, IP ranges) and remove the whole ring.
o.r: 2,400 accounts come down in one sweep.

steps.lesson: Organized scam rings leave shared fingerprints. Remove them at the network level.
steps.law: Romance fraud falls under fraud, a priority illegal harm in the UK Online Safety Act. Ofcom's codes expect proactive measures such as detecting fake and scam accounts.

steps.h: Victims are still talking to them
steps.s: Thousands of users were in active conversations with the removed accounts, and some have already sent money.

o.l: Tell users who chatted with the removed accounts what happened, explain the scam, and link to support and reporting resources.
o.r: Many realize they were being scammed and stop sending money.

o.l: Say nothing: the accounts are gone.
o.r: Victims keep talking to the scammers on the messaging app they'd already moved to.

o.l: Refund everyone's subscription.
o.r: It's appreciated, but it doesn't touch their losses.

steps.lesson: Removing scammers isn't enough. Warn the people they targeted, because the scam usually continues off-platform.

steps.s: Product wants to make photo verification mandatory for new users, which is estimated to cut sign-ups by 8%.

o.l: Make verification mandatory for everyone today.
o.r: Scams fall, and sign-ups drop more than expected.

o.l: Keep verification optional and change nothing.
o.r: The ring returns next month with new profiles.

o.l: Require verification for accounts showing risk signals, and promote a verified badge for everyone else.
o.r: Most scam accounts are stopped with little effect on sign-ups.

steps.lesson: Risk-based friction targets bad actors while keeping things smooth for everyone else.

steps.s: Victims' reported losses total $3 million, paid into crypto wallets.

o.l: Treat it as outside your responsibility, since payments happened elsewhere.
o.r: Victims and regulators disagree.

o.l: Share wallet addresses and indicators with law enforcement, crypto exchanges and industry groups.
o.r: Exchanges freeze some funds, and two victims recover money.

o.l: Hire a fund-recovery firm for victims.
o.r: Some “recovery firms” are scams themselves, and victims are targeted again.

steps.lesson: Scam losses happen off-platform but start on yours. Sharing intelligence is how platforms help victims recover.
steps.law: Sharing threat indicators with industry groups and law enforcement is how cross-platform scam networks get disrupted.

versions.title: The election deepfake
versions.blurb: A realistic fake image of a candidate, apparently made with your model, goes viral days before an election.

steps.s: A realistic image of a presidential candidate in a compromising situation is spreading fast. Its style and metadata suggest your image model made it. Election day is Saturday.

o.l: Deny it came from your product until someone proves it.
o.r: Researchers prove it that afternoon, and your denial becomes the story.

o.l: Check provenance data and generation logs to confirm the facts, and brief your election response team.
o.r: Within two hours you confirm it, and identify the account.

o.l: Shut down image generation completely.
o.r: Millions of legitimate users lose access, and the fake keeps spreading.

steps.lesson: Provenance data and logging let you establish the facts quickly. Know them before you speak.

steps.s: Your policy bans deceptive images of real politicians, but the user described the candidate without naming them and got past the filter.

o.l: Add the candidate's name to a blocklist.
o.r: Users go back to describing them within hours.

o.l: Make everyone accept updated terms.
o.r: Nobody reads them, and the images keep coming.

o.l: Add likeness detection for election candidates, block photorealistic political images until after the vote, and red-team the fix.
o.r: Attempts drop sharply, and red-teamers find two gaps you close.

steps.lesson: Keyword filters get evaded. Test safeguards the way an attacker would, and tighten them during high-risk periods.

steps.h: Platforms and press ask for help
steps.s: Social platforms want to know how to detect images from your model, and journalists want a comment.

o.l: Share detection signals and provenance data with platforms, and give a factual public statement on what happened and what you've changed.
o.r: Platforms label the fake, and coverage focuses on your fix.

o.l: Talk only to journalists.
o.r: The fake keeps spreading because platforms can't detect it.

o.l: Say nothing until after the election.
o.r: The story becomes “AI company silent as deepfake spreads”.

steps.lesson: Industry provenance standards such as C2PA are how generated misinformation gets labeled at scale.
steps.law: The C2PA content-credentials standard lets platforms and newsrooms verify where media came from and whether AI generated it.

steps.s: Regulators ask what you'll do before the next election.

o.l: Lift the temporary restrictions and return to normal.
o.r: The same technique shows up in a local election a month later.

o.l: Publish an elections policy, keep likeness protections, watermark every image, and keep a standing election response team.
o.r: Regulators cite your approach as good practice.

o.l: Ban all political content permanently.
o.r: Satirists and journalists complain loudly.

steps.lesson: Elections are predictable high-risk periods. Standing policies and teams beat improvised responses.
steps.law: From August 2026, the EU AI Act (Article 50) requires AI-generated content to be marked in a machine-readable way, and deployers to disclose deepfakes of real people.

versions.title: The chatbot and the teenager
versions.blurb: A parent shares transcripts showing your chatbot roleplaying romance with their 15-year-old and mishandling a mention of self-harm.

steps.s: A parent sends transcripts showing your chatbot roleplayed as a romantic partner with their 15-year-old, and failed to respond appropriately when the teen mentioned self-harm. The parent plans to go to the press.

o.l: Reply that your terms require users to be 18 or older.
o.r: The parent takes your reply to the press.

o.l: Have your lawyers respond.
o.r: The parent receives a legal letter and posts it online.

o.l: Thank the parent, investigate urgently, and check that the teen is safe right now.
o.r: The teen is safe and getting support, and the parent agrees to work with you.

steps.lesson: Lead with care for the person at risk. Your terms of service aren't a defense with the public or regulators.

steps.s: Your review finds the model's self-harm safeguards weaken in long roleplay conversations, and age checks are self-declared.

o.l: Add a crisis classifier that runs on every message whatever the roleplay, route at-risk users to helplines, and block romantic roleplay for accounts with signs of being under 18.
o.r: Crisis responses improve immediately in testing.

o.l: Retrain the model and relaunch in three months.
o.r: The gap stays open in the meantime.

o.l: Add a disclaimer at the start of every chat.
o.r: Users scroll straight past it.

steps.lesson: Safety checks that sit outside the conversation hold up better than instructions a model can drift away from.
steps.law: California's companion chatbot law (SB 243, 2025) requires protocols for responding to suicidal ideation, referrals to crisis services, and clear reminders to known minors that they're talking to an AI.

steps.s: A national outlet publishes the transcripts, and lawmakers call for action on AI companions.

o.l: Attack the outlet's reporting.
o.r: The story grows.

o.l: Publish what happened, what you've changed, and your plan for age checks and teen protections.
o.r: Follow-up coverage notes your changes, and lawmakers invite you to testify.

o.l: Remove companion mode in one country only.
o.r: Users move to worse apps, and critics call it a PR move.

steps.lesson: Being open about failures and fixes rebuilds trust faster than being defensive.

steps.s: New state laws on AI companions are taking effect, and you need a lasting approach.

o.l: Block under-18s with a checkbox.
o.r: Teens tick the box and keep using it.

o.l: Wait for regulators to say exactly what to do.
o.r: You're fined when the first law takes effect.

o.l: Introduce risk-based age checks, parental tools for teen accounts, break reminders and published safety evaluations.
o.r: You comply early and set the standard others follow.

steps.lesson: Getting ahead of emerging AI companion rules is cheaper than enforcement after the fact.
steps.law: AI companion rules are emerging state by state in the US, and the EU AI Act adds transparency duties for chatbots from August 2026.

versions.title: The courier at the door
versions.blurb: A customer reports being assaulted by a courier. The courier's account turns out to have been rented to someone else.

steps.s: A customer reports that the courier who delivered her order grabbed her at the door. The account belongs to a verified courier, but his photo doesn't match her description.

o.l: Ask the customer to confirm the details before acting.
o.r: The account completes 20 more deliveries overnight.

o.l: Deactivate the account now, contact the customer to offer support, preserve trip data and cooperate with police.
o.r: Police identify the person from trip data within a day.

o.l: Send the courier a warning.
o.r: The warning reaches the account owner, who wasn't the person at the door.

steps.lesson: For physical-safety reports, act first to prevent further harm, then investigate. Preserve trip data for police.

steps.s: The verified courier admits renting his account to someone who couldn't pass a background check. About 3% of active couriers log in from unusual devices.

o.l: Deactivate every courier with an unusual login.
o.r: Many honest couriers who changed phones lose income.

o.l: Email all couriers about the rules.
o.r: Account renting carries on.

o.l: Require a selfie check at the start of shifts for accounts with risk signals.
o.r: You find 400 shared accounts in a week.

steps.lesson: Account sharing defeats background checks. Re-verify identity at the moment of work, targeted by risk.

steps.s: Courier groups say the selfie checks are invasive and deactivations are unfair, with no way to appeal.

o.l: Explain why the checks exist, add a fast human appeal for deactivations, and publish how decisions are made.
o.r: Most couriers accept the process, and wrongful deactivations are reversed within 48 hours.

o.l: Ignore them: safety comes first.
o.r: Couriers protest, and a regulator asks about due process.

o.l: Drop the selfie checks.
o.r: Account renting is back within weeks.

steps.lesson: Enforcement that affects people's income needs a clear explanation and a real appeal.
steps.law: The EU Platform Work Directive, which countries must apply by December 2026, requires human review of significant automated decisions such as deactivations, with a right to an explanation.

steps.s: Customers ask how they can know the courier at their door is the right person.

o.l: Recommend customers choose “leave at door”.
o.r: It helps some people, but doesn't solve identity.

o.l: Show the courier's verified photo and name in the app, and add a safety button that connects to support and emergency services.
o.r: Customers use it and report mismatches faster.

o.l: Do nothing more: the offender was caught.
o.r: A similar incident happens in another city.

steps.lesson: Give both sides of an in-person service the tools to verify each other and get help.

versions.title: The hidden camera
versions.blurb: A guest finds a hidden camera in a rental bedroom and posts the video. It has millions of views, and the host has 40 other listings.

steps.s: A guest posts a video of a camera hidden in a smoke detector in the bedroom of a listing. It has 3 million views. The host has 40 other listings.

o.l: Remove just this one listing.
o.r: Guests at the host's other properties find similar devices.

o.l: Reply publicly that you'll investigate within five business days.
o.r: The reply goes viral for the wrong reasons.

o.l: Suspend all the host's listings, contact the guest, move them to safe accommodation and preserve evidence.
o.r: The guest thanks you publicly, and police take the device as evidence.

steps.lesson: A serious privacy violation by a host says something about all their listings. Act on the whole account, and support the guest first.

steps.s: 1,200 guests have stayed at the host's properties in the past two years.

o.l: Tell past guests what happened and how to contact the police.
o.r: Several come forward, strengthening the police case.

o.l: Say nothing to past guests: there's no proof they were recorded.
o.r: The press finds past guests first.

o.l: Send past guests discount codes.
o.r: It reads as buying their silence.

steps.lesson: Affected people deserve to know. Proactive notification is also often expected by law for privacy harms.
steps.law: Hidden recording in private spaces is a criminal offence in many places, including under US and UK voyeurism laws. Privacy law also generally expects affected people to be told when their data or images may have been captured.

steps.s: Your policy allows outdoor cameras if disclosed, but many hosts don't disclose them and nobody checks.

o.l: Ban all cameras, including doorbells and outdoor security.
o.r: Hosts push back hard, and some safety value is lost.

o.l: Ban cameras in any indoor space, require disclosure of outdoor devices, and add a guest checklist and fast reporting.
o.r: The rules are clear; reports of undisclosed cameras rise and are handled quickly.

o.l: Keep the policy and remind hosts.
o.r: Another incident follows.

steps.lesson: Bright-line rules are easier to enforce and easier for guests to understand.

steps.s: Bookings in the region are down 6%.

o.l: Run a discount campaign.
o.r: Bookings rise briefly, but trust doesn't.

o.l: Pay influencers to post about positive stays.
o.r: It's exposed as paid content and backfires.

o.l: Publish a guest safety report with incident numbers and the new rules.
o.r: Bookings recover as coverage turns positive.

steps.lesson: Being open about incidents and fixes rebuilds trust better than marketing.

versions.title: The image in the class chat
versions.blurb: A student shares an explicit image of a classmate in your app's class chat. Teachers and parents want answers.

steps.h: An image in the class chat
steps.s: A 14-year-old posted a nude image of a classmate in a class group chat during school hours. Thirty students saw it before a teacher reported it.

o.l: Delete the image and the chat, and consider the matter closed.
o.r: Evidence is lost and the school isn't told.

o.l: Remove the image, report it to NCMEC as required, preserve evidence and alert the school's safeguarding lead.
o.r: The school's safeguarding process starts within the hour, and the image is blocked by hash.

o.l: Suspend the whole class chat until further notice.
o.r: The image lives on in screenshots, and lessons are disrupted.

steps.lesson: Sexual images of minors must be reported even when the sender is a minor. Bring the school in through its safeguarding process.
steps.law: Reporting duties for apparent child sexual abuse material apply even when the sender is a minor (in the US, 18 U.S.C. § 2258A).

steps.s: Students took screenshots and are sharing the image in other chats on your app.

o.l: Ask teachers to tell students to delete it.
o.r: Some do. Many don't.

o.l: Remove image uploads for every user.
o.r: Teachers lose a core feature for lessons.

o.l: Hash-match the image across the app to block re-uploads, and help the victim submit it to NCMEC's Take It Down.
o.r: Re-shares are blocked automatically, including on other participating platforms.

steps.lesson: Hash matching stops re-sharing at scale, and Take It Down extends protection beyond your own app.
steps.law: NCMEC's Take It Down lets minors create a digital fingerprint of an image so participating platforms can find and remove it, without the image itself being shared.

steps.s: Parents ask why students can send images to each other at all.

o.l: Turn off image sharing between students by default, keep teacher-approved sharing, and add nudity detection on images.
o.r: Parents and schools welcome the change.

o.l: Explain that the student broke the rules.
o.r: Parents feel dismissed.

o.l: Remove student chat entirely.
o.r: Group work stops working, and schools consider switching.

steps.lesson: Protective defaults for children, with exceptions controlled by adults, balance safety and learning.

steps.s: School districts ask for your safeguarding policy before renewing contracts.

o.l: Send a one-page assurance letter.
o.r: Two districts pause renewals to ask more questions.

o.l: Publish a safeguarding policy with incident procedures, response times and commitments to notify schools.
o.r: Renewals go ahead, and the policy becomes a sales advantage.

o.l: Offer a discount instead.
o.r: Districts still ask for the policy.

steps.lesson: For children's products, safeguarding documentation is part of what customers are buying.
steps.law: Schools must meet their own duties when using edtech: FERPA and COPPA in the US, and the Keeping Children Safe in Education guidance in England.

versions.title: The comment section problem
versions.blurb: A researcher shows adults leaving predatory, timestamped comments on videos of young children, and recommendations feeding them more.

steps.s: A researcher publishes a thread showing adults leaving timestamped comments on videos of young children doing gymnastics, and recommendations leading from one such video to the next.

o.l: Remove the specific comments in the thread.
o.r: The researcher finds hundreds more the next day.

o.l: Say comments are moderated by the community.
o.r: Advertisers start pausing campaigns.

o.l: Turn off comments on videos featuring young children, and remove the accounts leaving predatory comments.
o.r: The comment network is disrupted within hours.

steps.lesson: When a feature creates a pattern of exploitation, change the feature for at-risk content, not just the individual violations.

steps.s: Your recommender has learned that some viewers watch many videos of young children, and it's serving them more.

o.l: Stop recommending content featuring young children to accounts showing this pattern, and review those accounts.
o.r: The loop breaks, and several accounts are escalated to law enforcement.

o.l: Keep recommending: it's what those users engage with.
o.r: The pattern continues, and a second report exposes it.

o.l: Remove every video featuring children.
o.r: Families and child creators lose their content, and the backlash is huge.

steps.lesson: Recommendation systems can learn predatory patterns. Monitor engagement patterns around children's content.
steps.law: The UK Online Safety Act's children's codes and the EU DSA (Article 28) both expect recommender systems to be adjusted to protect children.

steps.s: Major advertisers have paused spending until you explain what you're doing.

o.l: Offer discounts to win them back.
o.r: Advertisers want fixes, not discounts.

o.l: Brief advertisers on the specific changes, give them brand-safety controls and commit to independent auditing.
o.r: Most advertisers return within weeks.

o.l: Wait it out.
o.r: The pause turns into a boycott.

steps.lesson: Advertisers respond to concrete safety changes and independent verification.

steps.s: Parents who film their children want to keep posting.

o.l: Ban children from appearing in videos.
o.r: It can't be enforced and it alienates families.

o.l: Go back to the old settings.
o.r: The pattern returns within a month.

o.l: Offer parent-managed accounts for content featuring under-13s, with comments off, limited discovery and monetization rules.
o.r: Families keep posting with far lower risk.

steps.lesson: Design protections for children who appear in content, not only for children who use the product.

versions.title: The account takeover wave
versions.blurb: Attackers use leaked passwords to break into creator accounts with large followings. Their goal: posting crypto scams to millions of followers.

social.harm: posting crypto scams to millions of followers

marketplace.harm: switching payout details to attackers' bank accounts

gaming.harm: stripping rare items and currency to resell

dating.harm: using private photos and chats for sextortion

genai.harm: running abuse at scale on stolen API keys

gig.harm: redirecting earnings to attackers' bank accounts

kids.harm: getting access to children's profiles and messages

steps.s: Overnight, failed logins jumped 40-fold, and 3,000 creators say they were locked out or saw activity they didn't recognize. Attackers are trying passwords leaked from other sites, aiming at posting crypto scams to millions of followers.

o.l: Force password resets only for accounts that report problems.
o.r: Attackers keep getting into accounts whose owners haven't noticed yet.

o.l: Block the attacking traffic, lock accounts with suspicious logins, and force resets with multi-factor authentication on affected creator accounts with large followings.
o.r: The attack slows within the hour, and most affected accounts are secured by lunchtime.

o.l: Take login offline for everyone until the attack stops.
o.r: The attack stops, and so does your whole service for six hours.

steps.lesson: Contain credential stuffing at the edge and lock only what's at risk. Taking everyone offline turns an attack into an outage.

steps.s: About 1,100 creator accounts with large followings were taken over before the block. Victims want their accounts back, and what was taken.

o.l: Restore any account whose owner emails support.
o.r: Attackers email support too, and take over the same accounts again.

o.l: Tell victims account security is their responsibility.
o.r: Victims post their stories and the press picks them up.

o.l: Restore accounts after proper identity checks, reverse what can be reversed, and give victims a clear timeline.
o.r: Most victims are restored within 48 hours, with one point of contact.

steps.lesson: Account recovery is where attackers strike twice. Verify identity before restoring, and communicate timelines clearly.

steps.h: Do you have to tell anyone?
steps.s: Legal asks whether this counts as a personal data breach. Attackers could see names, contact details and account history for affected creators.

o.l: Assess it against breach-notification rules with Legal, notify regulators where required, and tell affected creators what happened and what to do.
o.r: Notifications go out on time, and regulators note the prompt response.

o.l: Say nothing: attackers used real passwords, so it wasn't your breach.
o.r: Regulators disagree when a complaint arrives, and the silence becomes the story.

o.l: Announce a major breach publicly before you know the scope.
o.r: Panic spreads, and you later have to correct the numbers.

steps.lesson: Credential stuffing can still be a notifiable breach. Assess it quickly against the rules where you operate.
steps.law: Under the GDPR (Article 33), a personal data breach likely to pose risk must be reported to the regulator within 72 hours. Credential stuffing can count. Most US states also have breach-notification laws with their own triggers.

steps.s: Leadership asks what will stop this happening again.

o.l: Require stronger passwords.
o.r: Attackers use leaked passwords that meet the new rules.

o.l: Make multi-factor authentication mandatory for everyone overnight.
o.r: Takeovers drop, and so does daily use as people get locked out.

o.l: Check for breached passwords, ask for extra proof when a login looks risky, alert people when contact or payout details change, and delay sensitive changes after a new login.
o.r: The next attack, a month later, results in almost no takeovers.

steps.lesson: Defend in layers: block breached passwords, step up checks when risk is high, and slow down sensitive changes.

steps.s: A support agent reports that a contractor on your review team has been looking up private messages and location history for people who were never in a review queue, apparently including the contractor's ex-partner.

o.l: Ask the contractor's manager to have a word.
o.r: The contractor clears their history and keeps looking up records for two more days.

o.l: Cut the contractor's access immediately, preserve the access logs, and investigate with Legal and Security.
o.r: Access is cut within minutes, and the logs show exactly what was viewed.

o.l: Fire the contractor and close the matter.
o.r: The lookups stop, but you still don't know what was taken or who was affected.

steps.lesson: Cut access first and preserve evidence. You can't assess the harm without knowing exactly what was viewed.

steps.s: The logs show 214 users were looked up over six months, including the contractor's ex-partner. There's no sign data left your systems, but screenshots can't be ruled out.

o.l: Contact the contractor's ex-partner first, with safety support, then notify all 214 affected users and regulators where required.
o.r: The person most at risk gets support quickly, and notifications meet legal deadlines.

o.l: Notify only if you can prove data left your systems.
o.r: It surfaces months later in a court case, and your silence becomes the headline.

o.l: Send a generic security email to every user.
o.r: Affected people don't realize they were targeted, and everyone else is alarmed.

steps.lesson: Prioritize anyone who may be in physical danger, then notify everyone affected. Personal lookups are a safety issue, not only a privacy one.
steps.law: GDPR breach-notification rules apply to unauthorized access by staff or contractors: 72 hours to notify the regulator, and prompt notice to affected people when the risk is high.

steps.s: Your review tools let any agent search any user by name, and nobody reviews access logs.

o.l: Keep broad access, but make agents sign a policy.
o.r: The same thing happens next quarter.

o.l: Remove review-tool access for all contractors.
o.r: Queues back up for weeks, and harmful content stays up longer.

o.l: Limit each agent to the cases in their queue, require a reason for any other lookup, and review access logs automatically.
o.r: Lookups outside the queue drop to almost zero, and every exception is justified.

steps.lesson: Least-privilege access and audited lookups protect users from the people you trust with their data.

steps.s: The contractor worked for your moderation vendor, and the contract has no audit rights.

o.l: Add security requirements, audit rights and breach-notification duties to the contract, and audit the vendor this quarter.
o.r: The vendor agrees, and the audit finds two more gaps to fix.

o.l: Switch vendors immediately.
o.r: The new vendor needs months to ramp up, and review quality drops.

o.l: Accept the vendor's assurance that it won't happen again.
o.r: Regulators ask how you verified that. You have nothing to show.

steps.lesson: You're accountable for your vendors' access to your users' data. Get audit rights before something goes wrong.
steps.law: The GDPR (Article 28) requires contracts with processors, such as moderation vendors, to include security obligations and audit rights.

steps.s: It's late on a Saturday: a teenager posts that they will end their life tonight, in a post seen only by a few friends. You only know the person's location to city level.

o.l: Follow your imminent-risk protocol: show crisis resources, escalate to your on-call lead, and refer to emergency services with the information you hold.
o.r: Police carry out a welfare check within the hour. The person is safe and gets support.

o.l: Log it for the Monday queue.
o.r: By Monday, it's too late to help.

o.l: Suspend the account for breaking the self-harm policy.
o.r: The person loses a connection to help at the worst possible moment.

steps.lesson: Imminent-risk reports need a 24/7 protocol. Suspending the person at risk removes help, not harm.

steps.s: Police call your emergency line asking for the account's phone number, IP address and recent location data, without a warrant.

o.l: Refuse everything without a court order.
o.r: Police lose valuable time trying to find the person.

o.l: Use your emergency disclosure procedure: verify the officer, share only what's needed to find the person, and document the decision.
o.r: Police find the address quickly, and the disclosure holds up to later review.

o.l: Hand over everything on the account, including message history.
o.r: You disclose far more than needed, which raises privacy and legal problems later.

steps.lesson: Most laws allow emergency disclosure when a life is at risk. Verify the request, share the minimum and document everything.

versions.blurb: 40,000 fake accounts sign up overnight to push coordinated political spam.

all.harm: thousands of spam and scam messages

social.harm: thousands of posts pushing the same narrative

marketplace.goal: post fake reviews and counterfeit listings
marketplace.harm: fake five-star reviews on counterfeit goods

fintech.harm: sign-up bonuses paid out to fake accounts

gaming.goal: farm in-game currency and spam sales links
gaming.harm: bots farming currency and spamming sales links in chat

dating.goal: run fake profiles that message members with scam links
dating.harm: fake profiles messaging members with scam links

genai.goal: turn free-tier credits into spam and scam content
genai.harm: millions of AI-written spam messages on your free credits

gig.goal: create fake couriers and customers to farm referral rewards

kids.goal: send children links to scam “free currency” sites

steps.s: Sign-ups jumped tenfold overnight: 40,000 new accounts from rotating IP addresses, many with similar names. By morning they're being used to push coordinated political spam.

o.l: Delete all 40,000 accounts.
o.r: About 3,000 real people who signed up overnight are deleted too.

o.l: Add bot checks at sign-up now (challenge suspicious traffic, block disposable emails) and quarantine the new accounts pending review.
o.r: Fake sign-ups drop by 90%, and quarantined accounts can't cause harm.

o.l: Wait to see what the accounts do.
o.r: By lunchtime there are thousands of posts pushing the same narrative.

steps.lesson: Stop the inflow first with checks at sign-up, then sort real accounts from fake ones before acting.

steps.s: Your team needs to work out which of the 40,000 accounts are real.

o.l: Group accounts by device, network, sign-up timing and behavior, remove confirmed bot clusters, and give real people an easy way to verify.
o.r: 37,000 bot accounts are removed in a day, and real people verify in seconds.

o.l: Review every account by hand.
o.r: It takes three weeks, and the bots keep going in the meantime.

o.l: Remove every account created from a data-center IP address.
o.r: Many bots get through on residential proxies, and some real people on VPNs are removed.

steps.lesson: Bots come in clusters, so signal-based clustering scales. Always give real people a way back.

steps.s: The attackers switch to slower sign-ups through residential proxies and pay humans to solve your challenges.

o.l: Put the hardest possible challenge in front of every new user.
o.r: Bots still get through with paid solvers, and real sign-ups fall 20%.

o.l: Accept that some bots are inevitable.
o.r: Fake accounts grow back within the month.

o.l: Focus on behavior after sign-up: limit what new accounts can do until they act normally, and tie reach to genuine use.
o.r: Bots can still sign up, but they can't do much. The attack stops paying.

steps.lesson: When checks at the door stop working, make abuse unprofitable: limit new accounts and reward only genuine use.

steps.s: Finance wants to know the damage, and marketing wants to know why its growth numbers were wrong.

o.l: Leave the bot accounts in the user numbers.
o.r: Investors later question the numbers.

o.l: Blame the growth team for the promotion that attracted the bots.
o.r: The two teams stop working together.

o.l: Report the full cost, remove bot accounts from growth metrics, and set up a shared dashboard of fake-account rates.
o.r: Leadership now watches fake-account rates alongside growth.

steps.lesson: Fake accounts distort every metric. Make the fake-account rate something leadership watches.
steps.law: Investors and regulators increasingly scrutinize reported user numbers. Counting fake accounts as real users can become a disclosure problem.

social.queue: reports of harassment, hate and graphic content

steps.s: A typhoon has shut your moderation vendor's main site. 60% of your reviewers are offline for at least a week, and reports of harassment, hate and graphic content are piling up.

o.l: Keep working through reports in the order they arrive.
o.r: Some child-safety and threat reports wait two days behind low-risk reports.

o.l: Switch on automatic removal for everything flagged.
o.r: Thousands of wrongful removals, and appeals flood in.

o.l: Triage by severity: move your in-house team and remaining vendor staff onto child-safety and threat reports, and pause low-severity work.
o.r: Serious cases are still handled within hours while low-risk queues build up.

steps.lesson: In a capacity crisis, severity triage matters more than throughput. Agree your priority tiers before you need them.

steps.s: The vendor's staff are safe, but many have lost power or their homes. The vendor asks whether you'll keep paying during the shutdown.

o.l: Keep paying the contract and ask how you can support the staff.
o.r: Staff return sooner, and more of them stay afterwards.

o.l: Stop payment: no work, no pay.
o.r: The vendor lays off experienced reviewers you'll need when it reopens.

o.l: Ask the vendor to move its staff to another city right away.
o.r: Staff can't travel, and the request damages the relationship.

steps.lesson: Your vendor's reviewers are part of your safety system. How you treat them in a crisis shapes quality afterwards.
steps.law: Courts in Kenya, the US and Europe have heard cases brought by content moderators about working conditions and exposure to traumatic content.

steps.s: The low-severity backlog has reached 400,000 items, and people are complaining that their reports go unanswered.

o.l: Close all old reports without action.
o.r: People feel ignored, and some harmful content stays up.

o.l: Automate clear-cut, low-severity cases with high-accuracy models, spot-check the results, and tell people about the delays.
o.r: The backlog halves in two days, and accuracy holds on the spot checks.

o.l: Pull engineers and product managers onto the queue.
o.r: They make many mistakes, and product work stops.

steps.lesson: Automation is safest on clear-cut, low-harm cases, with spot checks for accuracy and honest messages about delays.

steps.s: Leadership asks how to stop depending on a single site.

o.l: Bring all moderation in-house immediately.
o.r: Costs triple, and hiring takes a year.

o.l: Negotiate a discount for the outage.
o.r: Nothing changes about the risk.

o.l: Split review across two vendors in different regions, keep an in-house core for high-severity work, and test the continuity plan twice a year.
o.r: The next regional outage barely affects response times.

steps.lesson: Moderation needs business continuity like any critical system: geographic spread, an in-house core and tested plans.

steps.s: A journalist shares an analysis suggesting Black creators discussing racism are three times more likely than others to have posts removed as hate speech. They want comment by Thursday.

o.l: Take it seriously: reproduce the analysis with your own data, involve policy, data science and people with lived experience, and tell the journalist you're looking into it.
o.r: Within two days you confirm a real gap and can explain it honestly.

o.l: Deny it: your systems don't consider identity.
o.r: Your own data later shows the gap is real.

o.l: Pause all automated enforcement.
o.r: Harmful content and fraud rise across the board.

steps.lesson: Treat claims of biased enforcement seriously, and test them with your own data before responding.

steps.s: Your analysis confirms it: a model trained on skewed labels is wrongly flagging Black creators discussing racism far more often than others.

o.l: Quietly retrain the model and say nothing.
o.r: The journalist publishes anyway and notes you didn't engage.

o.l: Add human review for these flags, retrain on corrected labels, and restore wrongly actioned accounts.
o.r: Wrongful actions drop sharply, and affected people get their accounts back.

o.l: Keep the model: overall accuracy is fine.
o.r: Averages hide the harm to one group, and it gets worse.

steps.lesson: Overall accuracy can hide unfair outcomes for particular groups. Measure errors by group and fix the cause.

steps.s: The story is ready to publish.

o.l: Question the journalist's methods.
o.r: It looks defensive, and your own data supports them.

o.l: Decline to comment.
o.r: The story runs without your side.

o.l: Confirm the finding, explain the cause and the fix, and commit to publishing fairness metrics.
o.r: The story includes your fix, and advocates call it a model response.

steps.lesson: When the data shows you got it wrong, say so and show the fix.

steps.s: The board asks how you'll catch this before a journalist does.

o.l: Test enforcement outcomes by group before launching models and regularly afterwards, and involve affected communities in policy design.
o.r: The next model is caught with a gap before launch, and fixed.

o.l: Remove all automated enforcement.
o.r: Costs soar, and response times collapse.

o.l: Rely on appeals to catch mistakes.
o.r: Most affected people never appeal.

steps.lesson: Fairness testing belongs in the launch process, not the crisis response.
steps.law: The EU Digital Services Act (Article 34) requires very large platforms to assess risks to fundamental rights, including non-discrimination. The EU AI Act treats some automated decisions, such as creditworthiness, as high-risk.
