versions.title: The recalled toy
versions.blurb: A toddler is hospitalized after swallowing magnets from a toy bought on your marketplace. The toy was recalled months ago.

steps.s: A parent reports their toddler was hospitalized after swallowing small, powerful magnets from a toy bought on your marketplace. Regulators recalled the toy four months ago, and 300 listings from 40 sellers are still live.

o.l: Remove the one listing the parent bought from.
o.r: The other 299 listings keep selling.

o.l: Remove every listing matching the recalled product, stop pending orders, and contact the parent to offer support.
o.r: Every matching listing is down by noon, and 60 pending orders are stopped before shipping.

o.l: Ask sellers to confirm their stock isn't the recalled version.
o.r: Most don't reply, and sales continue for a week.

steps.lesson: When a product can hurt children, remove first and verify later. One report usually points to many listings.

steps.s: 2,100 people bought the toy in the past four months. Many are parents of young children.

o.l: Email past buyers directly with the recall notice, how to get a refund, and what to do if a child may have swallowed a magnet.
o.r: Parents return the toy, and a poison-control center thanks you for the clear guidance.

o.l: Post the recall notice in your help center.
o.r: Almost none of the buyers see it.

o.l: Leave it to the manufacturer to contact buyers.
o.r: The manufacturer doesn't have buyers' contact details. You do.

steps.lesson: Marketplaces often hold the only contact details for buyers. Use them to reach people when there's a safety recall.

steps.s: The consumer-safety regulator asks why recalled products were still listed four months after the recall.

o.l: Say sellers are responsible for what they list.
o.r: The regulator reminds you of your own obligations and opens an inquiry.

o.l: Explain honestly, and commit to checking listings against official recall databases daily, with automatic removal of matches.
o.r: The regulator accepts the plan and schedules a follow-up.

o.l: Promise to review every listing by hand.
o.r: It's impossible at your scale, and the regulator knows it.

steps.lesson: Checking listings against official recall databases is a basic control for any marketplace selling physical goods.
steps.law: The EU General Product Safety Regulation (applied since December 2024) requires online marketplaces to act on authorities' orders about dangerous products within two working days. In the US, the Consumer Product Safety Commission coordinates recalls and can pursue sellers of recalled products.

steps.s: Children's products, electronics and cosmetics account for most of your safety incidents.

o.l: Treat all categories the same.
o.r: The next incident is another children's product.

o.l: Stop selling children's products entirely.
o.r: Legitimate sellers leave, and buyers go elsewhere.

o.l: Require safety certificates from sellers in high-risk categories, and screen new listings in those categories before they go live.
o.r: Unsafe listings in those categories drop sharply.

steps.lesson: Put your strongest controls on the categories where products can physically hurt people.

versions.title: The review factory
versions.blurb: A competitor sends proof that a rival seller is paying for thousands of five-star reviews through a private group.

steps.s: A seller sends screenshots of a private group where people are paid $10, refunded after posting, for each five-star review of a rival seller's products. About 3,000 reviews look connected.

o.l: Ignore it: competitors complain about each other all the time.
o.r: The scheme grows, and a consumer group publishes the same screenshots.

o.l: Investigate the reviews using purchase patterns, refunds and reviewer networks, and freeze the rival's ratings while you do.
o.r: Within two days you confirm 2,600 paid reviews.

o.l: Suspend the rival seller immediately on the competitor's word.
o.r: Some screenshots turn out to be fabricated, and the seller sues.

steps.lesson: Tips from competitors are useful but aren't proof. Investigate with your own data before acting.

steps.s: The evidence is clear: 2,600 reviews were paid for, and the seller made $400,000 from the boosted sales.

o.l: Remove the fake reviews, suspend the seller, and hold their payouts while you decide on refunds.
o.r: The listings drop out of the rankings, and money is held back for affected buyers.

o.l: Remove the fake reviews but keep the seller.
o.r: The seller buys a new batch of reviews next month.

o.l: Leave the reviews up and warn the seller.
o.r: Buyers keep relying on fake ratings.

steps.lesson: Paid reviews defraud buyers. Remove them and act against the account that paid for them.

steps.s: Most of the 900 reviewers are real people who were paid. Some post paid reviews for many sellers.

o.l: Ban all 900 reviewers.
o.r: Many were one-off participants, and you lose real customers.

o.l: Remove their reviews, ban the repeat reviewers who work for many sellers, and warn one-time participants.
o.r: The professional reviewers are gone, and most one-time participants stop.

o.l: Take no action against reviewers.
o.r: The same reviewers are hired by other sellers next week.

steps.lesson: Tell professional review farms apart from one-off participants, and act in proportion.

steps.s: Fake reviews are now banned by consumer-protection law in the US, UK and EU, with fines attached.

o.l: Let only verified buyers review, detect review bursts and refund patterns, and publish your review policy.
o.r: Paid-review schemes become much harder, and regulators see a documented program.

o.l: Hide review counts.
o.r: Buyers trust the ratings even less.

o.l: Rely on buyers to report fake reviews.
o.r: Most fake reviews are never reported.

steps.lesson: Review integrity is now a legal requirement in many markets, not only a quality issue.
steps.law: The US FTC's 2024 rule on consumer reviews bans fake reviews and review suppression, with civil penalties. The UK's Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act (fake-review rules in force from April 2025) and EU consumer law also ban fake reviews.

versions.title: The sanctions near-miss
versions.blurb: Customers have been sending money to crypto wallets that were just added to a sanctions list, and three transfers are pending.

steps.s: Twelve crypto wallets were added to the US sanctions list overnight. Customers sent $2.4 million to two of them in the past month, and three transfers to them are pending right now.

o.l: Block the pending transfers, freeze the accounts involved while you review, and escalate to your compliance officer.
o.r: No new money reaches the sanctioned wallets, and compliance begins its review within the hour.

o.l: Let the pending transfers go through: they started before the listing.
o.r: They complete after the listing took effect, which is itself a violation.

o.l: Close every account that has ever sent crypto.
o.r: Thousands of legitimate customers lose access, and complaints flood in.

steps.lesson: Sanctions apply from the moment of listing. Screen against updates in near real time and stop pending payments.
steps.law: US sanctions administered by OFAC are strict liability: violations can be penalized even without intent. Blocked or rejected transactions must generally be reported to OFAC within 10 business days.

steps.s: Compliance confirms the earlier transfers happened before the listing, but the pending ones were blocked after it.

o.l: File the required reports on the blocked transfers within the deadline, with a clear timeline.
o.r: The regulator acknowledges the report and takes no further action.

o.l: Say nothing, because no money reached the wallets.
o.r: A later audit finds the unreported blocks, and the penalty is worse for the silence.

o.l: Report everything to every regulator worldwide.
o.r: It creates confusion and extra work with no benefit.

steps.lesson: Blocked sanctioned transactions often have to be reported too. Know the reporting duties everywhere you operate.

steps.s: Two of the frozen customers look like legitimate small businesses, and one was a victim of a scam run through the sanctioned wallet.

o.l: Keep everyone frozen indefinitely.
o.r: Legitimate businesses can't pay staff, and complaints reach the regulator.

o.l: Review each case quickly, unfreeze clearly legitimate customers, and help the scam victim report to police.
o.r: Legitimate customers are back within days, and the scam victim thanks you.

o.l: Unfreeze everyone to reduce complaints.
o.r: One of them turns out to be linked to the sanctioned network.

steps.lesson: Sanctions freezes need fast case-by-case review, so legitimate customers aren't punished for a match.

steps.s: Your screening checked customers at sign-up, but never the addresses they send money to.

o.l: Keep screening customers only at sign-up.
o.r: The same gap is exploited again.

o.l: Screen every outgoing payment against updated sanctions lists, and use blockchain analytics for crypto addresses.
o.r: The next listing is caught automatically within minutes.

o.l: Stop supporting crypto transfers.
o.r: Customers leave for competitors.

steps.lesson: Sanctions screening has to cover transactions and counterparties, not just customers at sign-up.

versions.title: The coerced customer
versions.blurb: A live-in carer appears to be draining an 84-year-old customer's account, and she insists everything is fine.

steps.s: An 84-year-old customer's account shows $38,000 in new cash withdrawals and transfers to a new payee over six weeks. A new phone number and email were added last month. The payee is her live-in carer.

o.l: Do nothing: she authorized the payments.
o.r: The account is nearly empty two weeks later.

o.l: Pause large transfers to the new payee, and have a trained specialist call her alone on her original phone number.
o.r: On the call, she mentions being frightened of the carer.

o.l: Close the account to stop the losses.
o.r: She loses access to her pension and bills, and the carer opens a new account elsewhere.

steps.lesson: Financial abuse of older people often hides behind “authorized” payments. Talk to the customer alone, through a channel you trust.

steps.s: She's frightened, but won't report the carer, who is her only help at home.

o.l: With her consent, involve adult protective services, add extra checks on large payments, and give her a named contact at the bank.
o.r: Social services arrange other care, and the transfers stop.

o.l: Respect her decision and do nothing more.
o.r: The abuse continues.

o.l: Report the carer to police without telling her.
o.r: She feels betrayed and stops talking to you.

steps.lesson: Respect the customer's choices while reducing harm: involve safeguarding services and add protections with her agreement.
steps.law: In the US, the Senior Safe Act (2018) protects trained financial staff who report suspected elder financial exploitation in good faith, and many states require or allow reports to adult protective services.

steps.s: The carer calls, angry that payments are blocked, and says he has power of attorney.

o.l: Take his word for it and unblock the payments.
o.r: He has no such document.

o.l: Tell him you suspect abuse.
o.r: He becomes aggressive toward her at home.

o.l: Ask for the legal document and have your legal team verify it before changing anything.
o.r: The document doesn't exist.

steps.lesson: Verify any claimed legal authority, and never share your suspicions with a suspected abuser.

steps.s: Your team realizes there's no process for spotting or handling financial abuse.

o.l: Rely on staff judgment.
o.r: The next case goes unnoticed.

o.l: Create a vulnerable-customer policy with abuse indicators, trained specialists, trusted-contact options and links to local safeguarding services.
o.r: The team spots three more cases the following quarter.

o.l: Block all transfers for customers over 80.
o.r: It's discriminatory, and customers complain.

steps.lesson: Financial abuse needs a defined process: warning signs, trained staff and trusted contacts the customer chooses.
steps.law: The UK Financial Conduct Authority's Consumer Duty expects firms to identify customers in vulnerable circumstances and adapt how they treat them.

versions.title: The recreated attack
versions.blurb: A user-built world recreating a real mass shooting is trending among teenage players.

steps.s: A user-built world recreating last month's mass shooting, with the attacker's manifesto on the walls, has 80,000 visits, mostly from teenagers. A news outlet has just noticed.

o.l: Take the world down, preserve it as evidence, and ban the creator's account.
o.r: It's gone within minutes, and copies are blocked by matching the world's assets.

o.l: Add an age warning to the world.
o.r: Visits double, and the story is about your warning label.

o.l: Review it on Monday with the policy team.
o.r: Copies spread across the weekend.

steps.lesson: Content glorifying real attacks should come down immediately, with evidence preserved and copies blocked.

steps.s: Twelve copies have appeared. The creator belongs to a group that has built other extremist worlds and recruits players into a private chat server.

o.l: Remove copies as they're reported.
o.r: New copies appear faster than the reports.

o.l: Match copies by shared assets and scripts, remove the group's other worlds, and refer the recruitment to law enforcement and industry partners.
o.r: The group's presence is removed in one sweep, and industry partners are alerted.

o.l: Shut down world-building for everyone this weekend.
o.r: Millions of legitimate creators are blocked.

steps.lesson: Extremist content comes from networks. Match copies by their parts and act against the whole network.
steps.law: GIFCT's hash-sharing database and Content Incident Protocol help platforms block copies of attack-related content quickly. In the EU, the Terrorist Content Online Regulation requires removal within one hour of an authority's order.

steps.s: 80,000 players visited, many of them young, and some joined the recruitment server.

o.l: Do nothing more: the content is gone.
o.r: Some young players are drawn further into the group elsewhere.

o.l: Show visitors a message with counter-extremism resources, and redirect searches about the attack to credible information.
o.r: Several parents contact counter-extremism services for help.

o.l: Ban all 80,000 visitors.
o.r: Curious teenagers are punished, and parents are furious.

steps.lesson: People exposed to extremist content may need redirection and support, not punishment.

steps.s: Leadership asks how to catch the next one before it trends.

o.l: Require approval for every new world.
o.r: Reviews take weeks, and creators leave.

o.l: Rely on player reports.
o.r: The next world reaches 50,000 visits first.

o.l: Check new worlds' names, text and assets against extremist indicators, and review fast-rising worlds before they reach recommendations.
o.r: Two similar worlds are caught before they trend.

steps.lesson: Proactive detection plus a check before content is amplified catches harm before it spreads.

versions.title: The $3,000 bill
versions.blurb: A 12-year-old spends $3,000 on loot boxes in two weeks, the parent's post goes viral, and a regulator starts asking questions.

steps.s: A parent's card statement shows their 12-year-old spent $3,000 on randomized item packs in two weeks, using a saved card. The parent posts it online and it goes viral.

o.l: Refuse: the purchases were made with a saved card.
o.r: The story spreads, and a regulator takes notice.

o.l: Refund the purchases, contact the parent, and add a spending limit to the child's account.
o.r: The parent posts an update thanking you.

o.l: Refund quietly and ask the parent to delete the post.
o.r: The parent posts your request too.

steps.lesson: When children overspend, generous refunds and immediate controls cost far less than the damage to your reputation.

steps.s: Your data shows 4% of under-16 players spent more than $500 last year, and purchases don't require a password.

o.l: Leave it to parents to set up controls.
o.r: Few parents know the controls exist.

o.l: Stop selling to under-18s entirely.
o.r: Children lie about their age, and revenue falls without solving the problem.

o.l: Require a password or parent approval for every purchase by under-18s, with monthly spending limits on by default.
o.r: Big spends by children drop sharply, with little effect on adult revenue.

steps.lesson: Protections that are on by default work better than controls parents don't know about.
steps.law: The FTC's 2022 settlement with Epic Games included $245 million in refunds for design that let children make purchases without parental consent.

steps.s: A consumer regulator asks whether your randomized packs are designed to pressure children into buying, and whether the odds are disclosed.

o.l: Answer openly, publish drop odds, remove countdown timers and “last chance” prompts for children, and show purchase history clearly.
o.r: The regulator closes the inquiry with recommendations.

o.l: Argue that loot boxes aren't gambling.
o.r: The regulator notes you didn't answer its questions.

o.l: Remove randomized packs in that one country.
o.r: Regulators elsewhere take note.

steps.lesson: Regulators focus on design that pressures children. Disclose odds and remove manipulative prompts.
steps.law: Belgium treats paid loot boxes as gambling, Australia rates games with paid loot boxes at least M (from September 2024), and Brazil's ECA Digital bans loot boxes for minors.

steps.s: Product is planning a new season with a limited-time pack.

o.l: Launch it as planned.
o.r: Complaints from parents spike again.

o.l: Review the design for manipulative patterns before launch, and build in child protections.
o.r: The season launches with fewer complaints and steady revenue.

o.l: Cancel the season.
o.r: Players are disappointed and revenue falls.

steps.lesson: Build a design and safety review into every launch aimed at young players.

versions.title: The 15-year-old on the app
versions.blurb: A member reports that their match says she's 15. The account has matched with 40 adults.

steps.s: A member reports that their match said she's 15 and in high school. Your app is 18+ with self-declared ages. The account has matched with 40 adults and is chatting with several.

o.l: Ask the user to confirm her age.
o.r: She says she's 18 and keeps chatting.

o.l: Suspend the account right away, and review its conversations for adults who carried on after learning her age.
o.r: You find two adults who kept pursuing her after she said she was 15.

o.l: Ignore it: users must be 18 under your terms.
o.r: An adult arranges to meet her.

steps.lesson: Treat reports of minors on adult platforms as urgent child-safety cases.

steps.s: Two adult members kept pursuing her after she said she was 15, and one asked to meet.

o.l: Warn the adults.
o.r: One of them contacts her on another app.

o.l: Ban both and delete their data.
o.r: The evidence police need is gone.

o.l: Ban both, preserve the evidence, and report them to NCMEC or the police.
o.r: Police open an investigation into the adult who asked to meet.

steps.lesson: Adults who pursue someone they know is a minor must be reported, with evidence preserved.
steps.law: Adults who pursue a user they know is a minor may be committing enticement offences, which US providers must report to NCMEC under the 2024 REPORT Act.

steps.s: Her account is suspended, and you can reach her by email.

o.l: Send a kind message explaining why the account was closed, with links to support services for young people.
o.r: She replies that she hadn't realized the danger.

o.l: Send a standard terms-violation notice.
o.r: She opens a new account with a different birthday.

o.l: Try to contact her parents directly.
o.r: You don't know who they are, and you risk exposing her.

steps.lesson: Communicate with care when minors break age rules. The goal is their safety, not punishment.

steps.s: Your data suggests about 0.5% of new sign-ups may be under 18.

o.l: Add a stronger warning to the sign-up form.
o.r: Minors click straight past it.

o.l: Require ID uploads from every user.
o.r: Many adults drop out, and minors borrow adults' IDs.

o.l: Add age estimation at sign-up when risk signals appear, detect language suggesting a user is a minor, and add “may be under 18” as a report reason.
o.r: Suspected minors are caught much earlier.

steps.lesson: Age assurance works best in layers, with extra checks where risk signals appear.
steps.law: Ofcom does not consider self-declaration of age to be effective age assurance under the UK Online Safety Act.

versions.title: The location leak
versions.platform: Dating app popular with LGBTQ people
versions.blurb: A researcher shows your “distance away” feature can pinpoint members' homes, including in countries where being gay is a crime.

steps.s: A security researcher shows that by checking the “distance away” figure from three fake locations, anyone can pinpoint a member's home to within 10 meters. Your app is widely used by LGBTQ people, including in countries where same-sex relationships are criminalized.

o.l: Ask the researcher not to publish while you fix it next quarter.
o.r: The researcher publishes in 30 days as planned, with the flaw still open.

o.l: Thank the researcher, round and blur distances today, and block the rapid location changes the attack relies on.
o.r: The attack stops working the same day.

o.l: Threaten legal action against the researcher.
o.r: The story becomes about you silencing a researcher.

steps.lesson: Location data can put lives at risk. Fix precision flaws immediately and work with the researcher.

steps.s: Members in countries that criminalize same-sex relationships face the greatest danger if they're located.

o.l: Keep the same settings for everyone.
o.r: Advocacy groups warn members to stop using the app.

o.l: Pull out of those countries overnight.
o.r: Members lose a lifeline, often with no warning.

o.l: Turn off distance display by default in those countries, offer a hidden-location mode, and add a discreet app icon option.
o.r: Advocacy groups praise the changes.

steps.lesson: Protect members in the most dangerous places by default, working with local advocacy groups.

steps.s: Logs suggest the technique may have been used against some members in the past year.

o.l: Say there's no evidence of harm.
o.r: Researchers later show it was used.

o.l: Investigate the logs, notify members who may have been targeted with safety advice, and inform data-protection regulators.
o.r: Members can take precautions, and regulators note the prompt notification.

o.l: Delete the logs to limit liability.
o.r: That's destruction of evidence.

steps.s: Leadership asks how to stop location features creating risks in future.

o.l: Add a privacy and safety review for every location feature, with threat modeling for stalking and for targeting of marginalized groups.
o.r: The next location feature ships with protections built in.

o.l: Remove all location features.
o.r: Matching gets worse, and members leave.

o.l: Rely on bug-bounty reports.
o.r: An attacker finds the next flaw first.

steps.lesson: Threat-model location features for stalking and persecution before they ship.

versions.title: The viral jailbreak
versions.blurb: A prompt that tricks your model into giving weapons instructions is spreading on social media.

steps.s: A prompt that tricks your model into giving detailed instructions for improvised weapons is circulating on social media with screenshots of the output. It's been shared 20,000 times.

o.l: Block the exact prompt text.
o.r: Users paraphrase it within minutes.

o.l: Deploy an output classifier for weapons instructions as an emergency patch, and red-team variations of the jailbreak.
o.r: The technique and its variations stop working by the afternoon.

o.l: Take the model offline until it's retrained.
o.r: Millions of users lose service for weeks.

steps.lesson: Fix the harmful output, not just the prompt. Jailbreaks change faster than blocklists.

steps.s: 30,000 accounts tried the prompt. A few hundred went on to ask follow-up questions about targets and materials.

o.l: Review the small group with concerning follow-ups, suspend where warranted, and refer credible threats to law enforcement.
o.r: Two accounts with credible threats are referred, and police act on one.

o.l: Ban all 30,000 accounts.
o.r: Most were curious people testing a viral prompt, and the bans cause a backlash.

o.l: Take no action on accounts.
o.r: One of the concerning accounts is later linked to an attack plot.

steps.lesson: Separate the curious from the concerning. Focus enforcement on behavior that suggests real intent.

steps.s: A newspaper asks how safe your model is, and policymakers cite the incident in AI safety debates.

o.l: Say every AI model can be jailbroken.
o.r: It's true, but it sounds like an excuse.

o.l: Decline to comment.
o.r: The story runs with the screenshots and no response.

o.l: Explain what happened and what you fixed, and publish your red-teaming approach and results.
o.r: Coverage notes the quick fix, and experts cite your disclosure.

steps.lesson: Being open about safety testing builds credibility when failures happen.

steps.s: Leadership wants to catch the next jailbreak before it goes viral.

o.l: Rely on user reports.
o.r: The next jailbreak is found on social media first.

o.l: Run continuous red-teaming, watch live traffic and jailbreak communities for known patterns, and track the jailbreak success rate as a key metric.
o.r: The next jailbreak is caught internally within a day.

o.l: Make the model refuse anything about chemistry or weapons.
o.r: Students and researchers can't use it, and complaints soar.

steps.lesson: Treat jailbreak defense as an ongoing program with metrics, not a one-off fix.
steps.law: The EU AI Act requires providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk to run adversarial testing and report serious incidents to the EU AI Office.

versions.title: The cloned voice
versions.blurb: Your voice tool was used to clone a teenager's voice for a fake kidnapping call to her parents.

steps.s: Police contact you: a family received a call in their daughter's cloned voice, crying for help, followed by a ransom demand. The clone was made with your tool from a video on her social media.

o.l: Suspend the account that made the clone, preserve all logs and audio, and give police what they need through your legal process.
o.r: Police trace the payment account linked to the user.

o.l: Point out that your terms forbid impersonation.
o.r: Police get nothing useful, and the family goes to the press.

o.l: Delete the cloned voice.
o.r: Evidence is lost.

steps.lesson: When your tool is used in a crime, preserve evidence and support the investigation quickly.

steps.s: Your tool can clone any voice from 30 seconds of audio, with no check that the speaker agreed.

o.l: Add a checkbox saying “I have permission”.
o.r: Everyone ticks it.

o.l: Shut down voice cloning permanently.
o.r: Legitimate uses, such as preserving the voices of people losing their speech, disappear.

o.l: Require consent from the speaker: a live recorded statement from the person being cloned, matched against the sample.
o.r: Cloning other people's voices becomes much harder.

steps.lesson: Verifying the speaker's consent is the key safeguard for voice cloning. A checkbox isn't consent.

steps.s: A review finds cloned voices of politicians and CEOs being used in scam calls and fake endorsements.

o.l: Remove the specific clones you found.
o.r: New ones are made the same day.

o.l: Block cloning of known public figures, add inaudible watermarks to all generated audio, and give banks and platforms a detection tool.
o.r: Banks start flagging cloned audio in fraud calls.

o.l: Publish a warning about voice scams.
o.r: It helps a little.

steps.lesson: Watermarking and detection help the whole ecosystem, not only your platform.

steps.s: Lawmakers are proposing rules on voice cloning and AI impersonation.

o.l: Lobby against any regulation.
o.r: Your company becomes the example lawmakers point to.

o.l: Share your consent and watermarking approach with lawmakers, and meet disclosure rules early.
o.r: Your approach is cited in the draft rules.

o.l: Wait and see.
o.r: Rules arrive that are harder to meet at short notice.

steps.lesson: Helping shape sensible rules with working safeguards beats reacting to rules written after an incident.
steps.law: In 2024 the US FCC ruled that AI-generated voices in robocalls fall under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act. The EU AI Act requires AI-generated or manipulated audio to be disclosed.

versions.title: The party house
versions.blurb: A house booked for “a quiet family weekend” hosts a 200-person party that ends in a shooting.

steps.s: Police report a shooting at a 200-person party at a house booked through your platform for “a quiet family weekend”. Two people are injured. The booking was made yesterday by a 19-year-old with a new account.

o.l: Activate incident response: cooperate with police, preserve booking data, support the host and neighbors, and suspend the guest's account.
o.r: Police get the booking details quickly, and the host feels supported.

o.l: Wait for police to contact you.
o.r: Police struggle to identify who booked the house.

o.l: Issue a statement blaming the host for not supervising.
o.r: The host goes to the press, and other hosts lose trust in you.

steps.lesson: Violence linked to your platform needs a ready incident response: cooperate, preserve evidence, support those affected.

steps.s: The booking had classic warning signs: a new account, a young guest, a one-night Saturday stay, and a large house in the guest's own city.

o.l: Ban all guests under 25.
o.r: It's discriminatory and hurts legitimate young travelers.

o.l: Remind hosts to check their guests.
o.r: Hosts can't see the signals you can.

o.l: Flag bookings with party-risk signals, and block or add checks to the riskiest ones.
o.r: High-risk bookings drop sharply the next weekend.

steps.lesson: Platforms can see risk signals individual hosts can't. Use them before the booking is confirmed.

steps.s: Neighbors are angry and say the house has had parties before. Local officials are considering restricting short-term rentals.

o.l: Say the platform isn't responsible for how guests behave.
o.r: The city passes restrictions.

o.l: Set up a neighbor hotline that responds within an hour, and share party-enforcement data with officials.
o.r: Officials hold off on restrictions and work with you instead.

o.l: Offer the neighbors vouchers.
o.r: It seems tone-deaf after a shooting.

steps.lesson: Communities around rentals are stakeholders. A responsive channel for neighbors reduces harm and regulatory risk.
steps.law: Cities increasingly regulate short-term rentals. The EU Short-Term Rental Regulation (applying from May 2026) requires platforms to share activity data with local authorities.

steps.s: Leadership asks for a lasting approach.

o.l: Keep the current policy and handle incidents case by case.
o.r: Another party incident happens on a holiday weekend.

o.l: Ban parties, enforce the ban with risk-based booking checks and extra holiday-weekend measures, and remove guests who break it.
o.r: Party reports fall significantly.

o.l: Require every guest to pay a large deposit.
o.r: Legitimate guests book elsewhere, and organized party-planners pay the deposit.

steps.lesson: Pair clear rules with risk-based enforcement, especially on predictable high-risk dates.

versions.title: The listing that didn't exist
versions.blurb: Holiday travelers arrive at rentals that don't exist, after being talked into paying outside your platform.

steps.s: Twelve families arrive for holiday stays to find the addresses are empty lots or someone else's home. Each booking started on your platform, but the “host” offered a discount for paying by bank transfer.

o.l: Tell the families they broke the rules by paying off-platform.
o.r: Families are stranded, and the story trends.

o.l: Find emergency accommodation for the families tonight, and remove the fake listings and linked accounts.
o.r: Every family has somewhere to stay by midnight.

o.l: Remove the listings and deal with the families on Monday.
o.r: Families sleep in their cars.

steps.lesson: People in immediate need come first, even when they broke your rules.

steps.s: The fake listings used stolen photos of real properties, and the same bank details appear in messages across 80 listings.

o.l: Remove only the listings that get reported.
o.r: Holiday travelers keep arriving at empty addresses.

o.l: Suspend all new listings until after the holidays.
o.r: Real hosts lose bookings in peak season.

o.l: Search for listings with reused photos and the same payment details in messages, remove them, and warn guests with upcoming bookings.
o.r: You remove 80 listings and warn 300 guests before they pay.

steps.lesson: Scam listings share fingerprints such as reused photos and payment details. Hunt for them proactively.

steps.s: The families paid a total of $60,000 by bank transfer.

o.l: Reimburse the families from a goodwill fund, and share the scammers' bank details with banks and police.
o.r: Banks freeze two of the scammers' accounts.

o.l: Tell the families to contact their banks.
o.r: Most recover nothing.

o.l: Reimburse only families who complain publicly.
o.r: Word gets out, and trust falls.

steps.lesson: Supporting victims of scams that start on your platform is part of your trust promise.

steps.s: Leadership asks how to prevent fake listings.

o.l: Add “never pay outside the app” to booking confirmations.
o.r: Some guests notice it; most don't.

o.l: Require every host to meet staff in person.
o.r: It's too costly to scale.

o.l: Verify that new hosts own or manage the property, detect reused photos, and warn guests when messages mention paying elsewhere.
o.r: Fake listings and off-platform payment scams drop sharply.

steps.lesson: Verify property control for new hosts, and step into conversations at the moment of risk.
steps.law: The EU Short-Term Rental Regulation (applying from May 2026) requires hosts to show a registration number and platforms to check it, which is a useful signal against fake listings.

versions.title: The takedown order
versions.blurb: A government orders you to remove posts by journalists criticizing a government minister within 24 hours, citing a vague national security law.

social.demand: remove posts by journalists criticizing a government minister

marketplace.demand: remove listings for T-shirts with protest slogans

fintech.demand: freeze the accounts of a protest group's organizers

gaming.demand: remove a player-built memorial to protesters

dating.demand: remove profiles that identify as LGBTQ

genai.demand: stop the model discussing a historical massacre

gig.demand: block drivers' in-app messages about a planned strike

kids.demand: remove lessons about climate change for students in the country

steps.s: A ministry in a country where you have local staff orders you to remove posts by journalists criticizing a government minister within 24 hours. It cites a broadly worded national security law and hints at “consequences” for your staff.

o.l: Comply immediately and in full to protect your staff.
o.r: The demands expand the following week, and users learn you complied quietly.

o.l: Have lawyers review the order's legal basis and scope, assess the human-rights impact, and work out what the law strictly requires.
o.r: Your lawyers find the order goes further than the law allows. You have options.

o.l: Ignore it.
o.r: Your local office is raided and staff are questioned.

steps.lesson: Handle government orders through a consistent process: check the legal basis and scope, and assess the human-rights impact before acting.
steps.law: The Global Network Initiative Principles and the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights expect companies to read government demands narrowly and challenge overbroad ones. Under the EU Digital Services Act (Article 9), orders from EU authorities must state their legal basis and territorial scope.

steps.s: Legal says the order is overbroad, but your local staff face real risk.

o.l: Remove it worldwide to avoid trouble.
o.r: People everywhere lose access to legitimate posts, and you're criticized for censorship.

o.l: Pull your local staff out of the country overnight.
o.r: Staff lose their jobs, and some can't leave safely.

o.l: Restrict access only in that country and only where the law clearly applies, and formally challenge the rest.
o.r: The posts stay available elsewhere, staff are protected, and you keep your legal position.

steps.lesson: Restrict only what you're legally required to, only where it's required, and keep staff safety central to the plan.
steps.law: Restricting content in one country, rather than removing it globally, is standard practice for local-law demands. Record these restrictions in your transparency reporting.

steps.s: The people whose posts are affected don't know about the order.

o.l: Tell them what was restricted and why, unless the law forbids it, and explain how they can challenge it.
o.r: They can challenge the decision, and trust holds.

o.l: Say nothing, to avoid provoking the government.
o.r: People assume arbitrary censorship, and trust falls.

o.l: Post the order publicly on social media.
o.r: The government retaliates against your staff.

steps.lesson: Tell affected people where the law allows. It's a core part of accountability for government demands.
steps.law: The EU Digital Services Act (Article 17) requires a statement of reasons whenever content or accounts are restricted, including restrictions made because of a government order.

steps.s: Civil-society groups ask how you handle government demands.

o.l: Keep government requests confidential.
o.r: A leak reveals both the requests and your silence.

o.l: Publish government requests in a transparency report, including how many you complied with, narrowed or refused.
o.r: Researchers and advocates cite your report as a model.

o.l: Say you never comply with government requests.
o.r: It isn't true, and it's quickly disproved.

steps.lesson: Transparency reporting on government demands builds trust and discourages overreach.
steps.law: The EU Digital Services Act (Articles 15 and 24) requires transparency reports that include the orders received from authorities.

versions.blurb: You launch in a market covered by the UK Online Safety Act's children's safety duties in 90 days, and nobody has started on compliance.

all.duty: assess risks to users and put proportionate protections in place
all.lawnote: Most new online safety laws are enforced by a dedicated regulator that can fine a percentage of global turnover.

social.law: the UK Online Safety Act's children's safety duties
social.duty: complete a children's risk assessment and use highly effective age assurance to keep children away from the most harmful content
social.change: age checks and safer feeds for teens
social.lawnote: Ofcom's children's safety codes have applied since July 2025. Breaches of the Online Safety Act can be fined up to £18 million or 10% of qualifying worldwide revenue, whichever is higher.

marketplace.law: the EU General Product Safety Regulation
marketplace.duty: register a single contact point for product safety, act on authorities' orders within two working days, and make sellers show safety information on listings
marketplace.lawnote: The EU General Product Safety Regulation has applied since December 2024. Online marketplaces must act on authorities' orders about dangerous products within two working days.

fintech.law: the EU Instant Payments Regulation's Verification of Payee rules
fintech.duty: check the payee's name against the account before every euro transfer and show the customer the result
fintech.change: a name check before every transfer
fintech.lawnote: Under the EU Instant Payments Regulation, Verification of Payee has been mandatory for euro credit transfers since October 2025. A provider that skips the check can be liable for the resulting loss.

gaming.law: Brazil's Digital Statute of Children and Adolescents (ECA Digital)
gaming.duty: stop offering paid loot boxes to minors, add parental supervision tools and verify ages beyond self-declaration
gaming.change: removing loot boxes for younger players
gaming.lawnote: Brazil's ECA Digital, enacted in 2025, bans loot boxes in games aimed at or likely to be accessed by children and requires age verification beyond self-declaration.

dating.law: the UK Online Safety Act's illegal harms duties
dating.duty: assess and reduce the risk of priority offences such as fraud on your service, and act quickly on illegal content
dating.change: scam detection and blurred images by default
dating.lawnote: Ofcom's illegal harms codes have applied since March 2025. Fraud is a priority offence, cyberflashing is a criminal offence, and breaches can be fined up to £18 million or 10% of qualifying worldwide revenue.

genai.law: the EU AI Act's transparency rules
genai.duty: tell people when they're talking to an AI and mark AI-generated content in a machine-readable way
genai.change: AI disclosure labels and content marking
genai.lawnote: The EU AI Act's transparency obligations (Article 50) apply from August 2026. Breaches can be fined up to €15 million or 3% of global turnover.

gig.duty: give workers human review of significant automated decisions such as deactivations, and explain how algorithms affect their work
gig.lawnote: EU countries must apply the Platform Work Directive by December 2026. It bars platforms from deactivating workers based solely on automated decisions.

kids.duty: get separate parental consent before sharing children's data for advertising, and keep a written data-retention policy
kids.lawnote: The FTC's updated COPPA Rule required compliance by April 2026. Each violation can bring a civil penalty of more than $50,000.

steps.s: You launch in a market covered by the UK Online Safety Act's children's safety duties in 90 days. You'll need to complete a children's risk assessment and use highly effective age assurance to keep children away from the most harmful content. Nobody has started.

o.l: Wait for the regulator to publish more detailed guidance.
o.r: Guidance arrives with 30 days to go, and everything is rushed.

o.l: Ask engineering to build whatever seems necessary.
o.r: They build the wrong things, and the real gaps remain.

o.l: Run a gap assessment against each requirement, give every gap an owner, and set a delivery plan with milestones.
o.r: By week two you know exactly what's missing.

steps.lesson: Compliance starts with a gap assessment against specific requirements, each with a named owner.
steps.law: Ofcom's children's safety codes have applied since July 2025. Breaches of the Online Safety Act can be fined up to £18 million or 10% of qualifying worldwide revenue, whichever is higher.

steps.s: Product says age checks and safer feeds for teens will cut engagement by 5% and asks to do the bare minimum.

o.l: Design it to meet the law's intent, measure the impact honestly, and look for ways to reduce friction.
o.r: The impact ends up at 2%, and the design holds up to review.

o.l: Do the minimum that technically complies.
o.r: The regulator's first review finds it doesn't meet the law's intent.

o.l: Delay the launch in that market.
o.r: Competitors who complied take the market.

steps.lesson: Regulators judge whether you meet a law's purpose, not just its wording. Good design reduces the cost.
steps.law: Regulators increasingly assess outcomes. The UK Online Safety Act, the EU DSA and the EU AI Act all expect measures to be effective in practice, not only present on paper.

steps.s: Ofcom can ask for evidence of how you comply.

o.l: Rely on the product itself as evidence.
o.r: When asked, you can't show how decisions were made.

o.l: Document your risk assessment, decisions, testing and results in a form you could hand to a regulator.
o.r: A later information request is answered in days.

o.l: Have consultants write documentation after launch.
o.r: It doesn't match what you built.

steps.lesson: If it isn't documented, regulators will assume it wasn't done.
steps.law: Record-keeping is built into most of these laws: the Online Safety Act requires written risk assessments, and the EU AI Act and GPSR require technical documentation.

steps.s: You've launched. What keeps you compliant from here?

o.l: Treat the project as finished.
o.r: Six months later, product changes have quietly broken compliance.

o.l: Freeze the product in that market.
o.r: You fall behind competitors.

o.l: Build compliance checks into product reviews, monitor key metrics, and review the risk assessment at least once a year.
o.r: Compliance holds as the product changes.

steps.lesson: Compliance is an ongoing program tied to product change, not a one-off project.
steps.law: Several of these laws require reassessment when your service changes significantly, not only on a fixed schedule.
